text:
Jonas Weber: hey folks — for the unit econ dashboard slice-by-quant work, we need to lock down `quantization_profile` tagging in telemetry. right now I see mixed strings in the sandbox tables ("int8", "w8a8", "awq", "none"). can we align on a canonical schema + versioning?

Arjun Desai: +1. we’ve been treating “profile” as a bundle: method + target + calibration set + runtime knobs. needs to be stable across regions + model families.

Nadia Rahman: from pipeline side: easiest if it’s a single dimension string on metering events + a couple optional columns. but we have to watch cardinality — don’t want “profile” to include free-form params.

Karthik Iyer: what are we trying to answer exactly? finance will ask “savings” but product will ask “did quality drop”. we should separate (a) what profile was used at runtime vs (b) what was *configured* but maybe fell back.

Logan Wright: yeah. telemetry today has `runtime_config` (json-ish) and `model_id`, and we can add a normalized `quantization_profile`. suggestion:
- `quantization_profile` = stable ID like `qp_<method>_<bits>_<scheme>_v<major>`
- `quantization_profile_version` = semver string
- `quantization_method` (enum) + `weight_bits`/`activation_bits` (ints)
anything more detailed should live in a lookup table keyed by profile id.

Thomas Baird: +1000 on lookup table. if you embed “calibration=wiki2023” etc in the dimension we’ll explode pre-agg groups.

Arjun Desai: ok, propose:
- `quantization_profile`: human-readable stable slug (e.g. `awq-w4a16-v1`, `gptq-w4a16-v2`, `int8-w8a8-v1`)
- `quantization_profile_id`: UUID or short hash? (I prefer slug only if we can guarantee uniqueness)
- `quantization_profile_status`: `enabled|disabled|shadow|fallback`

Nadia Rahman: status is helpful but “shadow” is ambiguous. can we define a boolean: `quantization_applied` true/false? and a string `quantization_fallback_reason` when false.

Karthik Iyer: +1. also need `requested_profile` vs `applied_profile`. we sometimes request AWQ but end up FP16 due to unsupported seq len / kernel mismatch.

Logan Wright: careful: two profile columns doubles cardinality. but we can encode requested in trace logs and only meter applied? unit economics cares about what actually ran.

Jonas Weber: I think unit econ slice should be by *applied*. but we need a way to quantify how often we fail to apply (otherwise we’ll misattribute “no savings”). maybe a rate metric separate from the main dataset.

Mei Lin: pipeline can support both if we pre-aggregate differently:
- main cost table: group by `applied_quantization_profile` only
- quality/ops table: separate daily counts for `requested_profile` x `applied_profile` to compute adoption + fallback rates (but not exposed in the main dashboard by default)

Marissa Cole: from Console UX: I can show quant profile filter for internal users, but we should default to “All” and have a tooltip that profile is “applied at runtime”. for MVP I’d rather not expose requested vs applied in UI unless it’s stable.

Arjun Desai: agree. can we settle on naming then:
- `quantization_profile` = applied runtime profile slug
- `quantization_profile_requested` = optional, used only in ops/adoption dataset
- `quantization_applied` = bool (redundant if profile = `none`?)

Thomas Baird: redundant columns are fine; redundancy helps BI users. but define `quantization_profile='none'` as canonical for unquantized. do NOT allow nulls.

Nadia Rahman: +1. also please make sure we don’t have 10 different “none” values. I’ll add a normalization step.

Jonas Weber: about versioning: we need to interpret savings vs quality. if `awq-w4a16-v1` changes calibration or outlier handling, cost may stay same but quality changes. so profile version has to bump when quality-affecting changes happen.

Arjun Desai: semantics proposal:
- bump MAJOR when numerical behavior can change materially (new algorithm, new calibration, different clipping/outlier handling)
- bump MINOR when only perf changes (kernel selection, better packing) with no expected quality change (still might have tiny diffs)
- bump PATCH for bugfix that doesn’t change math (e.g. metadata / packaging)
we can document “expected quality delta” per version in a registry.

Karthik Iyer: but perf-only changes can still impact output if you change KV cache quantization etc. so maybe simpler: ANY change that can affect logits => MAJOR.

Logan Wright: I’d rather be conservative. finance wants stable meaning. so yes: if logits can change => MAJOR. if strictly implementation detail with bitwise-identical outputs (rare) => MINOR/PATCH.

Arjun Desai: ok that’s workable. for our current roadmap, most changes will be MAJOR anyway.

Jonas Weber: cool. re: “savings” attribution: we should compute it as delta vs baseline profile *for same model + region + tier*, otherwise mix shift will swamp it. Can we add a baseline mapping table like `model_id -> baseline_profile`?

Nadia Rahman: pipeline can join a small mapping table owned by Applied ML. but it must be time-versioned (baseline can change). we can store `effective_start_date`/`end_date`.

Thomas Baird: time-versioned tables are fine, but keep it low-cardinality (per model family + region maybe). don’t do per-customer.

Marissa Cole: for “Explain cost delta” panel, we can attribute changes to “quant profile adoption” using (a) adoption rate changes and (b) per-profile cost deltas. but it’ll be hand-wavy until we have controlled cohorts.

Karthik Iyer: suggest we add a note in the dashboard: “Quantization savings reflect observed blended cost differences; may include correlated effects (routing, cache, batch size). Use experiments/evals for causal.”

Jonas Weber: yup. also quality: we should hook profile version to eval runs. I can expose a link like `evalset:prod_prompts_v5` results by profile version.

Arjun Desai: action items:
1) I’ll draft a short “Quantization profile registry spec” (slug format + when to bump major)
2) Nadia/Logan: confirm telemetry fields + normalization rules
3) Mei: separate adoption/fallback dataset as discussed
4) Marissa: copy for tooltip + explain panel caveat

Nadia Rahman: works. for fields, I’ll propose:
- `quantization_profile` (string, non-null, canonical values from registry; default `none`)
- `quantization_profile_version` (string, semver; for `none` use `0.0.0`?)
- `quantization_method` (enum: `none|awq|gptq|int8|fp8` etc)
- `weight_bits` (int) + `activation_bits` (int) (nullable for none)
Requested/adoption stuff in a separate table.

Thomas Baird: prefer `quantization_profile_version` null when profile=none (avoid weird 0.0.0). but can live either way as long as consistent.

Logan Wright: +1 null is cleaner. but “no nulls” makes BI easier. tradeoff.

Jonas Weber: I’m ok with null version for none, but please make sure looker/semantic layer coalesces it to “none”.

Nadia Rahman: ok: in raw telemetry we’ll allow null version for none; in semantic layer we can coalesce `quantization_profile_version` to `""` and keep `quantization_profile='none'`.

Marissa Cole: :thumbsup: as long as filter options don’t show blank strings.

Arjun Desai: I’ll put in the registry doc: “none” is a valid profile with no version.

Jonas Weber: last thing: naming. can we standardize on `w4a16` etc in slug? also `bf16`/`fp16` should be treated as non-quant profiles (i.e. `none`).

Arjun Desai: yep. runtime precision (bf16/fp16) is separate; quant profile is only when weights/acts are quantized. so `none` covers bf16/fp16.

Karthik Iyer: good. otherwise we’ll confuse “precision” with “quantization”.

Nadia Rahman: ok I’ll take this back to the ingestion PR. expect a draft schema in a few hours.

Jonas Weber: thanks all. ping me on the registry doc; I’ll review for quality semantics.

Marissa Cole: (side note) once this lands, I’ll add a quick internal-only filter + add a chart “$/1M by quant profile” behind the feature flag.

Thomas Baird: pls add guardrails: max 20 profiles shown, rest bucketed as “other”, otherwise chart legend becomes unreadable.

Marissa Cole: yep, will do.

Logan Wright: closing loop: I’ll also add a metric for `quantization_profile_applied_rate` to the data quality checks so we can catch sudden drops (like kernel regression causing fallback to none).

Jonas Weber: perfect. that’s exactly what we need for rollout monitoring.
